你.etymology: Everyday singular second-person pronoun ('you'), combining the person classifier 亻 with 尔 (ěr), which itself served as a second-person pronoun in Classical Chinese. Attested in Northern Dynasties and Tang vernacular texts such as the Book of Zhou (Zhou Shu), 你 gradually replaced 尔 and 汝 as the standard spoken Mandarin pronoun among peers and colleagues.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 你 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 你 (via 萌典)

您.etymology: Polite singular second-person pronoun ('you'), formed by placing 你 ('you') above 心 ('heart') to signal respectful deference. Emerging in Jin and Yuan dynasty northern vernacular (originally fused from plural 你们 in polite address), 您 became Standard Mandarin's courteous pronoun for elders, teachers, and guests.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 您 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 您 (via 萌典)

我.etymology: First-person singular pronoun ('I, me'), attested since Late Shang oracle-bone inscriptions, where the graph depicted a notched polearm before being borrowed phonetically for the first-person pronoun. In Classical Chinese texts such as the Classic of Poetry (Shijing) and Analects, 我 already serves unchanged as both subject 'I' and object 'me'.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 我 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 我 (via 萌典)

他.etymology: Third-person singular masculine or general pronoun ('he, him'), formed from 亻 ('person') and 也. In Classical Chinese (Mencius, Zhuangzi), 他 (also written 它 or 佗) meant 'other, another person'; during the Tang dynasty it grammaticalized into the general third-person pronoun.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 他 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 他 (via 萌典)

她.etymology: Third-person singular feminine pronoun ('she, her'), written with the woman component 女 beside 也 and pronounced tā identically to 他. Introduced into modern written Mandarin in the late 1910s (popularized by poet and linguist Liu Bannong) to distinguish 'she' visually on the page while preserving spoken tā.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 她 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 她 (via 萌典)

我们.etymology: First-person plural pronoun ('we, us'), combining 我 ('I') with the human plural suffix 们 (men). Plural markers written 弭, 伟, 懣, and finally 們 appear in Song and Yuan vernacular literature to form collective personal pronouns.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 我們 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 我們 (via 萌典)

你们.etymology: Second-person plural pronoun ('you all'), combining 你 ('you') with the human plural marker 们 (men). Unlike French vous, Mandarin 你们 always addresses two or more people; polite singular respect uses 您 instead.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 你們 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 你們 (via 萌典)

他们.etymology: Third-person plural pronoun ('they, them'), formed from 他 ('he / person') plus the plural marker 们 (men). Used for male or mixed groups of people without any subject-versus-object case change.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 他們 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 他們 (via 萌典)

是.etymology: Equative copula ('be: am, is, are') linking two nouns or noun phrases. In Classical Chinese (Analects, Mencius), 是 originally functioned as the proximal demonstrative 'this' and adjective 'right, correct'; in Han-dynasty prose its résumé position between topic and predicate ('X, this [is] Y') reanalyzed into the modern copula 'be'.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 是 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 是 (via 萌典)

很.etymology: Degree adverb ('very') that also serves as the natural, unstressed link before simple predicate adjectives (今天很冷 'It is cold today'). In Classical Chinese (Shuo Wen Jie Zi, Zhanguo Ce), 很 meant 'unyielding, intractable, severe'; in Ming–Qing colloquial Mandarin that intensity bleached into the everyday degree word 'very'.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 很 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 很 (via 萌典)

好.etymology: Core adjective 'good, fine, well' (hǎo), combining 女 ('woman') and 子 ('child'). Already among the earliest graphs on Shang oracle bones and ubiquitous in the Classic of Poetry, 好 expresses quality, readiness (修好了 'fixed and ready'), and greetings (你好 'hello').

history.meaning: good; fine; lovely (hǎo); to be fond of (hào)

sources.title: Wiktionary — 好 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好 (via 萌典)

不.etymology: General negation adverb ('not, no') for present, future, habitual, and stative predicates, attested from Shang oracle bones through every stage of Chinese. Spoken bù shifts automatically to rising second tone bú immediately before another fourth-tone syllable (不是 bú shì).

sources.title: Wiktionary — 不 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不 (via 萌典)

没.etymology: Existential and past-completion negator read méi ('not have; did not'), written with the water component 氵. Under its literary reading mò ('sink, submerge'), the graph appears in Classical Chinese; by late Tang and Song lyric poetry (such as Wei Zhuang's ci), 沒 had grammaticalized in spoken Chinese to negate 有 and completed events.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 沒 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 沒 (via 萌典)

有.etymology: Verb of possession ('have') and existence ('there is, there are'), attested from Shang oracle bones and bronze inscriptions through Classical and modern Mandarin. Unlike every other Mandarin verb, 有 is always negated with 没 (没有), never 不.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 有 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 有 (via 萌典)

没有.etymology: Negative counterpart of 有 ('do not have; there is no; did not'), combining the negative 没 with 有. Established in Song–Yuan vernacular texts, 没有 both negates possession/existence before nouns and negates completed actions before verbs.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 沒有 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 沒有 (via 萌典)

在.etymology: Locative verb ('be at, in, on'), locative coverb ('at, in'), and progressive marker ('right in the middle of doing'). In Classical Chinese (Analects, Shijing), 在 already means 'reside in, be located at, exist'; modern Mandarin extends that 'being at a point' sense to ongoing actions before verbs.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 在 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 在 (via 萌典)

要.etymology: High-frequency verb and modal ('want, need, will / be going to'). Originally depicting two hands at the waist (later clarified as 腰 'waist'), 要 in Classical Chinese meant 'seek, invite, essential' (yāo / yào), from which vernacular Mandarin developed 'need, want' and imminent future 'be about to'.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 要 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 要 (via 萌典)

想.etymology: Mental and modal verb meaning 'think of, miss, would like to', combining 相 ('observe, mutual appearance', phonetic xiāng) above 心 ('heart-mind'). Attested in Han-dynasty texts for calling an image to mind, 想 before another verb expresses a polite wish ('would like to') softer than direct 要.

history.meaning: call to mind; long for; think

sources.title: Wiktionary — 想 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 想 (via 萌典)

需要.etymology: Compound verb and noun meaning 'need, require', pairing 需 ('await, require', attested in the Yijing) with 要 ('essential, need'). Used in polite requests and everyday explanations of what a task calls for.

history.stage: Classical roots in Yijing (需) & Mencius (要)
history.meaning: require + essential -> modern compound 需要 'need'

sources.title: Wiktionary — 需要 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 需要 (via 萌典)

了.etymology: Neutral-tone aspect and sentence particle le marking a completed action (after a verb) or a newly changed situation (at the end of a sentence). Grammaticalized during the Tang and Song dynasties from the full verb 了 (liǎo, 'finish, complete'), which is already illustrated in its particle sense in Su Shi's Song lyrics.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 了 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 了 (via 萌典)

吗.etymology: Sentence-final particle turning any declarative statement into a neutral yes/no question without changing word order. Grammaticalized in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular from earlier negative finals (such as 无 wú / 么 me appended at the end of a statement to ask 'or not?'), with 口 added to show its purely spoken particle role.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 嗎 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 嗎 (via 萌典)

呢.etymology: Sentence-final particle used for bounce-back follow-up questions ('And what about X?' 你呢？) and for highlighting an ongoing state ('right now'). Written with 口 ('mouth') plus 尼 (ní phonetic), its conversational particle uses are richly attested in Qing vernacular novels such as Honglou Meng.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 呢 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 呢 (via 萌典)

吧.etymology: Sentence-final particle softening commands into warm invitations ('let's…', 'go ahead and…') or asking for gentle confirmation. Formed with 口 ('mouth') + 巴 (bā phonetic) and evolved from earlier imperative/concessive finals like 罢 (bà, 'finish, let it be') in Ming–Qing colloquial speech.

history.meaning: final particle softening suggestions and assumptions

sources.title: Wiktionary — 吧 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 吧 (via 萌典)

的.etymology: Structural particle de linking an owner, noun, adjective, or clause to a following noun (我的书 'my book', 安静的院子 'quiet courtyard'), or forming a headless possessive ('mine, Teacher Song's'). In Tang–Song vernacular texts this linker was often written 底 (dǐ) before standardizing on 的 in Yuan–Ming prose.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 的 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 的 (via 萌典)

个.etymology: Mandarin's default general measure word (classifier) placed between a number or demonstrative and a noun (一个人, 这个房间). Originally counting stalks of bamboo (written 箇 with the bamboo radical 竹, or 個 with 亻 in Classical texts like Xunzi and Shiji), it broadened by the Six Dynasties and Tang period into a universal classifier.

morphemes.meaning: bamboo stalk / single unit -> general classifier

history.meaning: counter for bamboo shafts, arrows, individual items

sources.title: Wiktionary — 個 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 個 (via 萌典)

把.etymology: Measure word for objects you grip by a handle or back (一把钥匙 'a key', 一把椅子 'a chair') AND disposal coverb fronting a definite object before an action verb (把门打开). Both functions grew directly out of the Classical Chinese verb 把 ('grasp, hold in the hand', combining 扌 'hand' + 巴 phonetic).

history.meaning: hold or grasp in the hand
classifier for handled items; object-fronting marker

sources.title: Wiktionary — 把 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 把 (via 萌典)

间.etymology: Measure word for rooms of every kind (一间客房 'a guest room', 一间书房 'a study'), combining 门 ('doorway, gate') with 日 ('sunlight'). Depicting light peeking through a doorway gap, 間 in Classical Chinese meant 'interval, space between' and the bay between building pillars—hence one room.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 間 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 間 (via 萌典)

张.etymology: Measure word for flat, spread-out surfaces and paper items (一张桌子 'a table', 一张纸 'a sheet of paper', 一张床 'a bed'). Formed from 弓 ('bow') + 长 (cháng phonetic), 張 originally meant 'string and draw a bow open' in the Shijing, extending naturally to things spread flat.

history.meaning: classifier for flat sheets, tables, beds

sources.title: Wiktionary — 張 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 張 (via 萌典)

件.etymology: Versatile measure word counting upper-body clothing (一件外套 'a coat'), pieces of luggage (一件行李), and matters or affairs (一件事). Combining 亻 ('person') and 牛 ('ox'), Shuo Wen Jie Zi defines 件 as 'divide, distinguish into distinct items'.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 件 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 件 (via 萌典)

杯.etymology: Noun 'cup' and measure word for cupfuls or glassfuls of drinks (一杯热茶 'a cup of hot tea', 一杯咖啡 'a cup of coffee'). Written with 木 ('wood', reflecting early lacquered wooden drinking vessels) and 不 phonetic, 杯 is attested in Classical banqueting scenes in the Shiji and Mencius.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 杯 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 杯 (via 萌典)

双.etymology: Measure word for things that come in natural matched pairs (一双皮鞋 'a pair of leather shoes', 一双手 'a pair of hands'). The traditional graph 雙 shows two birds (隹 + 隹) held in one hand (又)—literally 'a matched pair held together'.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 雙 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雙 (via 萌典)

条.etymology: Measure word for long, narrow, or winding things: streets, lanes, rivers, towels, trousers, and legal clauses (一条老街 'an old street', 一条毛巾 'a towel'). In the Classic of Poetry, 條 originally named a long, slender tree branch, from which the long-strip classifier grew.

history.meaning: classifier for streets, rivers, ropes, clauses

sources.title: Wiktionary — 條 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 條 (via 萌典)

本.etymology: Measure word for bound books, notebooks, and ledgers (一本书 'a book', 一本账本 'a ledger'). Formed by marking the lower root of 木 ('tree') with a stroke, 本 meant 'tree root, foundation, origin' in Classical Chinese, then 'bound volume' once bamboo slips were superseded by stitched codices.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 本 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 本 (via 萌典)

位.etymology: Polite measure word for people—especially guests, teachers, and elders (一位客人 'a guest', 一位老师 'a teacher'). Combining 亻 ('person') and 立 ('stand'), 位 in Classical court texts named a person's proper standing place or seat of honor, naturally becoming a respectful counter.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 位 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 位 (via 萌典)

这.etymology: Proximal demonstrative ('this'), pairing with a measure word before nouns (这个 'this one', 这间房 'this room'). Written with the movement component 辶 plus 言, 這 emerged in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese (alongside earlier 者) to replace Classical 此 ('this').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 這 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 這 (via 萌典)

那.etymology: Distal demonstrative ('that'), pairing with a measure word before nouns (那个 'that one', 那条街 'that street') or opening a clause with 'well then'. Attested as a demonstrative in Han–Six Dynasties colloquial texts, contrasting directly with proximal 这.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 那 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那 (via 萌典)

哪.etymology: Interrogative determiner ('which?'), written with 口 ('mouth') beside 那 to distinguish rising third-tone nǎ ('which?') from falling fourth-tone nà ('that'). Followed by a measure word (哪个 'which one?', 哪间房 'which room?') or 里/儿 (哪里 / 哪儿 'where?').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 哪 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哪 (via 萌典)

哪里.etymology: Standard question word meaning 'where?', combining 哪 ('which?') and 里 ('inside, place'). Stays in the exact sentence slot of the answer rather than moving to the front: 电脑在哪里？ ('The computer is where?').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 哪裡 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哪裡 (via 萌典)

这里.etymology: Location pronoun meaning 'here' ('this place'), formed strictly parallel to 那里 ('there') and 哪里 ('where'). Placed right after 在 to anchor where someone or something is.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 這裡 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 這裡 (via 萌典)

谁.etymology: Interrogative pronoun 'who, whom' (shuí or shéi), combining 言/讠 ('speech, ask') with 隹 (zhuī phonetic). Already standard across Classical Chinese (Shijing, Analects), 谁 stays in place in Mandarin questions and takes 的 to form 谁的 ('whose?').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 誰 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 誰 (via 萌典)

什么.etymology: Everyday question word 'what?' (shén me), descended from Tang–Song vernacular 拾沒 / 什麼 ('what thing?'). Used standalone (什么？ 'What?') or directly before a noun (什么茶？ 'What kind of tea?').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 什麼 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 什麼 (via 萌典)

怎么.etymology: Interrogative adverb asking 'how?' or 'how come?' directly before a verb (怎么走？ 'how do I get there?', 怎么拿错了？ 'how did it get mixed up?'). Formed with the same colloquial -么 suffix as 什么 and attested throughout Ming–Qing vernacular fiction.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 怎麼 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 怎麼 (via 萌典)

一.etymology: Cardinal number 'one', written since oracle-bone antiquity with a single horizontal stroke. In spoken Mandarin, 一 undergoes regular tone sandhi: yī in counting and ordinals (第一), rising yí before a fourth tone (一个 yí gè), and falling yì before tones 1, 2, and 3 (一杯 yì bēi).

sources.title: Wiktionary — 一 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一 (via 萌典)

两.etymology: Word for 'two' used before measure words and paired nouns (两个房间 'two rooms', 两把钥匙 'two keys'). In Classical Chinese, 兩 denoted a matched pair (such as two chariot wheels) and a unit of weight, explaining why Mandarin prefers 两 when counting concrete items with classifiers while keeping 二 for abstract counting and ordinals.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 兩 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 兩 (via 萌典)

二.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'two', written since oracle-bone inscriptions with two parallel horizontal strokes. Used in counting ('one, two, three'), ordinals (第二 'second'), floor/room numbers (二楼 'second floor'), and multi-digit numbers (十二 'twelve', 二十 'twenty').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 二 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 二 (via 萌典)

请.etymology: Polite request marker ('please') and hospitality verb ('invite; treat someone to a meal'), combining 讠 ('words') with 青 (qīng phonetic). In Classical Chinese etiquette (Analects, Liji), 請 meant 'respectfully request permission or invite', which remains the heart of modern 请进 ('please come in') and 请坐 ('please sit').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 請 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 請 (via 萌典)

请问.etymology: Polite question opener ('excuse me, may I ask…'), pairing 请 ('respectfully request') with 问 ('ask'). Already attested as a courteous formula in Classical dialogues in Mencius ('Dare I respectfully ask…'), it remains Standard Mandarin's everyday way to approach a front desk or stranger.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 請問 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 請問 (via 萌典)

谢谢.etymology: Everyday expression of gratitude ('thank you'), formed by reduplicating 谢 ('thank, express gratitude; decline politely', written with 讠 'speech' + 射 phonetic). Single 謝 for thanking someone appears in Han-dynasty historical records (Shiji), while reduplicated 謝謝 became standard in Ming–Qing spoken Mandarin.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 謝謝 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 謝謝 (via 萌典)

再见.etymology: Standard Mandarin farewell ('goodbye', literally 'again see / meet again'), pairing 再 ('once more, again') with 见 ('see, meet'). Mirrors friendly 'see you again' expressions worldwide without restricting the time of day.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 再見 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 再見 (via 萌典)

对不起.etymology: Sincere everyday apology ('I'm sorry'), a potential-complement phrase literally meaning 'unable to face (you) squarely / let you down': 对 ('face, treat rightly') + 不 ('not') + 起 ('measure up'). Standardized in Qing and modern Mandarin alongside its classic reassuring reply 没关系 ('it doesn't matter').

history.meaning: have let someone down; 'I am sorry'

sources.title: Wiktionary — 對不起 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 對不起 (via 萌典)

没关系.etymology: Warm reassuring reply to an apology ('it doesn't matter; no problem'), combining 没 ('not have') with 关系 ('connection, bearing, consequence'—literally 'no bearing / nothing to worry over').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 沒關係 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 沒關係 (via 萌典)

你好.etymology: Universal Mandarin greeting ('hello'), built from 你 ('you') + 好 ('good, well'—originally a short wish '[may] you [be] well'). Because two third-tone syllables meet (nǐ + hǎo), the first naturally lifts to second tone in speech: ní hǎo.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 你好 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 你好 (via 萌典)

您好.etymology: Polite Mandarin greeting ('hello'), substituting respectful 您 ('you') for everyday 你 before 好 ('well'). Used when greeting guests at a front desk, teachers, or elders.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 您好 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 您好 (via 萌典)

早上.etymology: Everyday noun for 'morning' (early morning until around nine or ten o'clock), combining 早 ('early, dawn', attested throughout Classical Chinese) with the noun-forming time/location suffix 上. Pairs with 好 to form the warm greeting 早上好！ ('Good morning!').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 早上 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 早上 (via 萌典)

明天.etymology: Noun meaning 'tomorrow', combining 明 ('bright, next dawning', combining 日 'sun' + 月 'moon') with 天 ('day, sky'). Classical Chinese said 明日 ('next sun/day'); vernacular Mandarin replaced 日 with everyday 天 to form 明天.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 明天 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 明天 (via 萌典)

今天.etymology: Noun meaning 'today', combining 今 ('now, present', attested on Shang oracle bones and in the Shijing) with 天 ('day'). Parallels 昨天 ('yesterday') and 明天 ('tomorrow'), and sits before or right after the subject without any preposition.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 今天 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 今天 (via 萌典)

门.etymology: Core noun 'door, gate', descended directly from a Shang oracle-bone pictograph of two swinging wooden gate leaves under a lintel. Counted with the measure word 扇 (一扇门 'a door') and productive in compounds like 开门 ('open the door'), 门口 ('doorway'), and 大门 ('front gate').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 門 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 門 (via 萌典)

钥匙.etymology: Compound noun 'key' (yào shi, counted with 把: 一把钥匙), combining two metal-radical (钅/金) words: 钥 ('lock bolt / key') and 匙 ('key / spoon'). In Classical texts 鑰 named the metal bolt of a gate lock while 匙 named the key inserted to open it; vernacular Mandarin joined the pair into one disyllabic noun.

history.meaning: lock bolt + key -> compound 鑰匙 'key'

sources.title: Wiktionary — 鑰匙 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 鑰匙 (via 萌典)

茶.etymology: Mandarin word for 'tea' (chá), written with 艹 ('plant'), 人, and 木 ('tree'). Prior to the Mid-Tang dynasty, tea was written with the shared bitter-herb graph 荼 (tú); tea master Lu Yu's Classic of Tea (Cha Jing, c. 760) popularized removing one horizontal stroke to establish 茶—the ancestor of English 'tea' (via Hokkien tê) and 'chai' (via northern chá).

sources.title: Wiktionary — 茶 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 茶 (via 萌典)

水.etymology: Fundamental noun 'water' (shuǐ), descended from an oracle-bone pictograph of a flowing stream flanked by ripples and droplets. Serves both as an independent word (热水 'hot water', 喝水 'drink water') and as the left-hand component 氵 in hundreds of liquid-related characters.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 水 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水 (via 萌典)

房间.etymology: Everyday two-syllable noun for 'room' (counted with 间: 一间房间), pairing 房 ('side house, chamber', attested in the Shijing) with 间 ('architectural bay, room space').

sources.title: Wiktionary — 房間 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 房間 (via 萌典)

客栈.etymology: Traditional courtyard inn or boutique guesthouse (counted with 家: 一家客栈), combining 客 ('traveler, guest') with 栈 ('wooden gallery, storehouse, wayside lodge'). Historic 客棧 served merchants and travelers along imperial post roads and remain iconic in preserved old quarters of Chengdu and Southwest China.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 客棧 (Chinese)
MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 客棧 (via 萌典)
